extracted.intended_audience: power plant owners/operators, CCS and pipeline project developers, state regulators, environmental lawyers, and stakeholders participating in EPA rulemaking/notice-and-comment
extracted.subtask_description: EPA preamble analysis supporting the determination that carbon capture and storage (CCS) achieving 90% CO2 capture for coal-fired steam generating units is adequately demonstrated, and that CO2 transport via pipelines (and related permitting/rights-of-way) is feasible. The page synthesizes demonstrations, vendor statements, state laws, technical operational factors, pipeline examples, funding programs, and permitting processes to justify feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: State CCS Requirements as evidence of establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states encourage or even require sources to install CCS. These state requirements further indicate that CCS is well-established and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Illinois 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (zero emissions timelines and Clean Coal Portfolio Standard with capture-rate requirements up to 90%), Michigan 2023 clean energy requirement (defines “clean energy” to include 90% capture), California scoping plan and Assembly Bill 1279, Louisiana 2022 Climate Action Plan (defines 90% capture as qualifying clean energy), Pennsylvania Climate Action Plan and interagency workgroup, North Dakota and Wyoming gubernatorial initiatives and state laws requiring CCS on some coal plants. The preamble uses these statutes and planning frameworks to indicate industry confidence and regulatory support for deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable load, startups, and shutdowns do not prevent 90% capture achievability
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 capture plants can accommodate turndown and the duty cycles/startup/shutdown profiles of coal-fired steam generating units such that 90% capture over a year is achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes average coal unit duty cycles (~70%), demonstrated capture plant turndown limits (Boundary Dam ~60%, Petra Nova ~70%), achievable turndown to 50% for a single capture train (and down to 25% with two trains), data showing higher capture efficiencies at lower loads (e.g., Shand Feasibility Report: 97.5% capture at 62.5% net load where design achieves 90% at full load), low contribution of startup/shutdown to annual emissions (few startups per year, lower-carbon ignitor fuels, low heat-input rates), and incentives (IRC section 45Q) that encourage higher capacity factors and thereby fewer startups/shutdowns. Conclusion: startup/shutdown/variable load do not affect achievability of 90% capture over long periods (a year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability across coal ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: 90% CO2 capture is achievable across all coal ranks because amine solvents have been used with a broad range of flue gas compositions and capture systems can be designed to the appropriate scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting details: demonstrations on lignite (Boundary Dam, Milton R. Young), subbituminous (W.A. Parish), bituminous (Plant Barry, Warrior Run, Argus), and anthracite (Wilhelmshaven); typical coal-combustion flue gas CO2 concentrations vary only between ~13–15%; capture systems can be sized (absorber columns) and designed for different CO2 concentrations; flue gas impurities (SO2, NOx, PM, trace impurities) can be managed via existing controls or by adding FGD (costed in EPA analysis), polishing columns, or solvent reclaiming (e.g., activated carbon beds). The EPA concludes 90% capture is achievable across all coal ranks, including waste coal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-application of capture experience from natural gas-fired turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience capturing CO2 from natural gas-fired combustion turbines supports the determination that 90% capture from steam generating units is adequately demonstrated, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites information on CO2 capture from natural gas-fired turbines and explains that technology and operational lessons are transferable between turbine and steam-generating unit applications, strengthening the evidence base for 90% capture applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary rules regarding EPAct05-assisted projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EPA's interpretation of EPAct05, the Agency may not rely on EPAct05-assisted capture projects as the sole basis for a determination of adequate demonstration, but may rely on those projects to support or corroborate other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA lists the non-EPAct05 evidence sufficient by itself (Boundary Dam engineering analysis and other coal demonstrations, industrial applications, vendor statements, non-EPAct05 natural gas turbine experience). EPAct05-assisted projects provide substantial additional support but cannot be the sole basis for the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 transport by pipelines is adequately demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Operation of CO2 pipeline infrastructure in the U.S. for decades demonstrates that design, construction, and operational requirements for CO2 pipelines are adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA data: 8,666 km (5,385 miles) of CO2 pipelines in operation in 2022; pipelines have been used for nearly 60 years. The U.S. network includes trunklines and laterals; pipeline transport is the majority mode for CO2 and considered economical. EPA therefore concludes pipeline transport as a component of CCS is adequately demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance/proximity of sources to sequestration sites supports feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic proximity of coal-fired steam generating units to potential sequestration formations makes pipeline transport feasible for the majority of sources, enabling use of relatively short intrastate pipelines in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data from DOE/NETL: of coal-fired capacity planned to operate during/after 2039, 80% is within 100 km (62 miles) of potential deep saline sites and 91% within 160 km (100 miles). EPA projects ~8,000 km (5,000 miles) of pipeline would be constructed (not optimized) if each plant built a lateral to the nearest sequestration site; compliance modeling projects 3,300–4,700 miles of pipeline buildout. These buildout rates are comparable to historical pipeline construction and less than some annual natural gas pipeline construction ranges, supporting feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing and planned trunklines can reduce required new pipeline miles (but BSER analysis does not assume their buildout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing/planned CO2 trunklines could reduce new pipeline construction needs, but EPA’s BSER analysis is conservative and does not assume trunkline buildout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA lists existing networks (Cortez, Denbury pipelines, etc.) and announced projects (Summit Carbon Solutions Midwest Carbon Express, Wolf Carbon Solutions Mt. Simon Hub, Tallgrass conversions) that could lower costs and reduce miles to be constructed. However, BSER is premised on source-to-sequestration laterals and does not rely on future trunkline networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete pipeline project examples demonstrate technical feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous constructed pipelines of varying lengths and capacities demonstrate practical feasibility of CO2 pipeline construction and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Beaver Creek (76 km), Monell (52.6 km), Bairoil (258 km), Sheep Mountain (656 km), Cortez (808 km), Coffeyville-to-North Burbank (109 km), Terrell Gas to Permian Basin (132 km), Kemper County (96 km), Citronelle (19 km), Denbury trunklines (e.g., 232 miles). Capacities range from 1.6 to 27 million tons/year and uses include EOR and saline storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPAct05-assisted CO2 pipelines as corroborating demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 pipelines constructed with EPAct05 funding provide additional evidence of pipeline construction and operation capability, usable as supporting corroboration (not sole basis per EPAct05 interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Illinois Industrial Carbon Capture and Storage, Petra Nova (131 km pipeline), Red Trail Energy, Project Tundra (0.4 km lateral). Petra Nova restarted operations in 2023 and its pipeline and project history are discussed as supportive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding, FEED studies, and federal programs support pipeline/trunkline development
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal funding and programs (IIJA FEED grants, CIFIA, DOE funding) provide financial and planning support that facilitates CO2 pipeline and trunkline buildout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: IIJA-funded FEED studies (Wyoming Trails Carbon Hub, Gulf Coast 965 km system FEED), CIFIA ($2.1 billion to DOE for direct loans/loan guarantees/future growth grants) to finance shared transport infrastructure, and other IIJA programs intended to accelerate pipeline development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting and rights-of-way are manageable and vary by state
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipeline siting/permitting, landowner rights, and eminent domain authority are governed by state laws and vary by state; states have taken steps to facilitate siting and construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: state regulation determines siting and rights-of-way acquisition methods (voluntary easements or eminent domain if allowed); some states treat CO2 operators as common carriers/public utilities (important for eminent domain); 17 states explicitly allow eminent domain for CO2 pipelines; joint permit applications created by some states (IL, LA, NY, PA) streamline state and federal permitting; intrastate permitting generally quicker than interstate due to fewer state agencies involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA requirements and statutory timelines relevant to pipeline projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal actions (e.g., funding) normally trigger NEPA review (EA or EIS) and the Fiscal Responsibility Act set statutory deadlines for NEPA documents to accelerate review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An EA determines whether significant impacts exist and may lead to a FONSI; an EIS is required for actions with significant effects. Fiscal Responsibility Act amendments: EAs must be completed within 1 year and EISs within 2 years (lead agency may extend deadlines in consultation with applicant). NEPA applicability depends on project specifics (crossings of sensitive habitats, federal land, funding source). Examples: ADM Decatur pipeline required only an EA and was completed fairly quickly; Petra Nova required an EIS with a notice of intent in Nov 2011 and record of decision in May 2013 (under 2 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical acquisition of rights-of-way and ability to cross multiple land types
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipeline developers have successfully secured rights-of-way across private, state, and federal lands and through sensitive habitats, demonstrating practical ability to obtain ROW for CO2 pipelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Summit Carbon Solutions easement agreements with thousands of landowners and high percentage of ROW acquired across multiple states; Citronelle Project acquired ROW through forested timberland and wetlands and mitigated endangered species habitat impacts; Denbury Cedar Creek Anticline pipeline required easements across state trust lands, federal lands, and private lands and was completed in 2021. EPA uses these examples to show developers can navigate land acquisition complexities.
